name: Tomas Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the night-shift team lead at a city discount supermarket, so I'm in from ten at night to six in the morning. I lead a crew of five on restocking and on picking click-and-collect orders, and then I work the first tills for the early commuters. I use an AI assistant every day to plan the delivery pallets and to write up the incident log. I love the quiet of the aisles at 3am. What wears me out is how it wrecks my sleep and my social life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful, just not magic. I'd tell friends to try them for boring stuff first. At work I'd show the crew the stock planner, because it saves us about forty minutes a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the hype is a bit silly but the tools are already good enough for what I do. If nothing changes, I keep my job and keep getting better at it. My real risk is the self-checkouts that keep growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd go deeper on the tools. I'd build a small sheet that forecasts which items run out on which nights, and I'd show it to the area manager to get a pay bump. I'd also keep up the little side thing I do, reselling sneakers online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Steady and a bit bored, in a way that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now, and how much of that is a surprise to your boss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Priya (the store manager) knows about the stock planner and likes it. She doesn't know I use the AI to draft my own reports, but she wouldn't mind. The crew find it funny that I talk to my laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your money look in a world where nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay-ish. About 2,400 a month in my pocket, rent of 700 on a shared flat, and about four months saved. It's not rich, but nothing is on fire.

say: The tools are **useful**, just not magic.
I'd show the night crew the **stock planner**, since it saves forty minutes a shift.
think: The hype is silly, but tools are already **good enough** for my work.
My real risk is the **self-checkouts** that keep growing.
do: Go deeper on the tools and build a small **forecast sheet**.
Show it to the area manager and ask for a **pay bump**.
Keep reselling **sneakers** online on the side.
feel: **Steady**, a bit bored, and fine with that.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I keep my job and keep getting better at it.
fieldNote: Daily AI user who treats the **plateau** as a slow, useful upgrade.
Turns skill into bargaining power: a forecast sheet to win a pay bump.
Cushion is about four months, rent shared, nothing on fire.

steps.text: Build a forecast sheet for nightly stock-outs
Ask the area manager for a pay bump

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, learn the tools now and the change is easy. I'd tell the crew to learn at least the stock app. Online I'd post tips and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, forecasting and the incident log are all thinking tasks, and I do them with AI already. So I'm half ahead of it. The tills and shelves are slower. The crew who just stack boxes are the ones who'll feel it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose to my manager that I train the crew on the tools and become the person who runs them. I'd take an online course in inventory systems. I'd put the sneaker side hustle on a proper footing with a small online shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, with a bit of buzz. I'm curious, not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use the tools. What would software do to your night crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software will do the forecasting that I do now, and the pallet planning too, so I'd stop being the one who does the thinking. That's why I want to move up to running the systems, not just being a person who uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the move you'd make before your employer does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a title like night operations lead before the change, not after. If I'm the one who knows the system, they can't swap me for a new graduate. It's a bit cheeky, but cheeky works.

say: Learn the tools now and the change is **easy**.
I'd tell the night crew to learn the **stock app** at least.
think: Ordering and the incident log are **thinking tasks** I already do with AI.
The crew who only stack boxes will feel it **first**.
do: Pitch my manager to train the crew and **run the tools**.
Take an online course in **inventory systems**.
Turn the sneaker hustle into a small **online shop**.
feel: **Curious** and a little buzzed, not scared.
S1.quote: I'd ask for a title like night operations lead before the change, not after.
fieldNote: Wants to be the person who **runs** the systems, not the one replaced by them.
Worries for the crew who only stack boxes.
Asks for titles early; says cheeky works.

steps.text: Pitch the manager to train the crew on the tools
Take an online inventory systems course
Open a small online shop for the sneakers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, use the tools, and get a second income. I'd tell friends to pay off debts and keep cash. Online I'd write about how to prepare, not just panic about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's big. The thinking part of my job goes quickly, and then the physical part around 2031, with the robots. Night shelf stacking is exactly what a robot would do first, since there are no customers around to bother. I'm good at the thinking part, but that's the part that AI does better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd list everything I own and everything I owe, then cut costs to the bone. I'd pour my savings into building the online shop to a real income stream. Then I'd learn how to maintain the robots, and I'd ask the company now if it would fund a technician course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with an engine in it. I'd rather be moving than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first week after hearing 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say 2,400 a month, rent of 700, and four months saved. I'd go to 1,500 a month in costs, so my cushion becomes six months. If the shop makes 400 a month, that's another cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your sense of safe look like when robots come three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots would do exactly what my crew does at night, so I'd have until about 2031 before the shelves are done by machines. That's three years to move into maintaining them or running the systems. I'd bet on being the person who fixes the robot.

say: Get ready now: use the tools, pay off **debts** and build a second income.
I'd write about how to **prepare**, not just panic.
think: The thinking part goes fast, then **robots** around 2031 take night shelf stacking.
I'm good at thinking tasks, but **AI does them better**.
do: List everything I own and owe, then cut to **1,500 a month**.
Pour savings into the **online shop** to make it real income.
Ask the company to fund a **technician course**.
feel: **Anxious**, but with an engine in it; moving beats waiting.
S2.quote: Night shelf stacking is exactly what a robot would do first, since there are no customers around to bother.
fieldNote: Fear becomes a **plan** in the first week: costs, shop, technician route.
Names the exact task most exposed, his own crew's night stacking.
Bets on fixing robots instead of competing with them.

steps.text: Cut monthly costs to 1,500 to build six months of savings
Put savings into growing the online sneaker shop
Ask the company to fund a robot-technician course
Use AI daily to learn maintenance basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now. I'd tell friends to get a second skill and a second income. At work I'd offer to teach the crew the tools on my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be excited. I'd be 32 in 2031, and the robots come around 2034, so I'd have time to be good at something that they need. Maybe I'm lucky to start with the tools already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening technician course, 18 months, then ask to move into equipment maintenance. I'd grow the shop with the 200 a month I'm saving. I'd use AI daily to learn the electronics side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good, a little nervous. It'd feel like the start of a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still switch to the technician route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, still the technician route. With more time I'd also look at store-systems jobs, because supermarkets will need people who connect the robots to the stock software. That's where my forecasting sheet becomes a CV line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shop and the supermarket job fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop would pay for the course and the supermarket job would pay the rent while I study. By year three I'd hope the shop covers half my costs. Then I'd choose which one I keep.

say: Five years is **enough** if you start now.
I'd tell friends to get a **second skill** and a second income.
think: I'd be 32 in 2031, with robots around **2034**, so there's time to get good at what they need.
Starting with the tools already feels like **luck**.
do: Do an 18-month **evening technician course**, then ask to move into maintenance.
Put **200 a month** into growing the shop.
Use AI daily to learn the **electronics** side.
feel: Fairly **good**, a little nervous, like the start of a project.
S3.quote: By year three I'd hope the shop covers half my costs. Then I'd choose which one I keep.
fieldNote: Five years turns the problem into a **project** with milestones.
Notes that supermarkets will need people linking robots to stock software.
The shop pays for study, the supermarket pays the rent.

steps.text: Do an 18-month evening course in equipment maintenance
Put 200 a month into the online shop
Use AI to learn electronics basics
Apply for store-systems jobs once qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years, so it's a game of who prepares. I'd tell the younger crew to learn something every year. I'd also back a retraining scheme for low earners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel calm, and I'd probably build things more slowly. I'd be 37 in 2036 and the robots in 2039, so I could be in a very different job by then. I want to be doing something that I chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study part-time to become a store-systems technician, and I'd grow the shop to a small business. I'd save for a flat deposit and maybe start a family around 32. I'd go on using AI each day, since it's already my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, hopeful. I'd even be a bit excited about the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What do you do differently when you're not in a rush?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more risks, like launching a second shop line and taking a short course in coding. Without a rush I can afford to try things and drop the ones that don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be running a small online business and working a few days in tech support for stores. Probably living with my partner in a flat of our own, and sleeping at night. Sleeping at night would be a big win.

say: Ten years is a game of **who prepares**.
I'd tell younger crew to learn something **every year** and back a retraining scheme.
think: I'd feel **calm** and build more slowly, with time to end up in a job I chose.
Robots in 2039 may leave me in a **different job** altogether.
do: Study part-time to become a **store-systems technician**.
Grow the shop into a small **business**.
Save for a **flat deposit** and maybe start a family.
feel: **Calm** and hopeful, even a bit excited about the robots.
S4.quote: I can afford to try things and drop the ones that don't work.
fieldNote: With a decade, he shifts from defence to **ambition**: a business, a flat, a family.
Treats AI as an edge he already has.
Wants sleep at night as much as career change.

steps.text: Study part-time to become a store-systems technician
Grow the online shop into a small business
Use AI every day to stay ahead of the crew

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because everything lands at once and my savings are only about four months. What would help is a company-funded technician course, a few months of income support while I study, and tax breaks for small online shops. I'd happily do the rest myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not typical. A lot of my crew don't use the tools and nobody's teaching them. If somebody came into the night shift and taught them for a week, it'd change a lot of lives.

headlineQuote: If somebody came into the night shift and taught them for a week, it'd change a lot of lives.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old **night-shift team lead** at a city discount supermarket, running restocking and click-and-collect picking.
He uses AI every day, runs a sneaker reselling side hustle and likes to move before his employer does.
He has about four months saved and rent of 700 on a shared flat.
He leans left, worries about the crew who don't use the tools, and plans a **technician** route into robot maintenance.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because everything lands at once on about four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A company-funded **technician course**, income support while studying, and tax breaks for small online shops.
